description: Dominant and contested representations, the rise of self-representation, and why representations matter socially.
content_html:
Dominant and Contested Representations

Not all representations are equal. Some become so familiar and so widely repeated across media that they begin to feel like simple descriptions of reality rather than constructed choices. These are dominant representations. A dominant representation does not need to be accurate to be powerful — it simply needs to be everywhere. When audiences encounter the same representation of a social group across news programmes, drama series, advertising campaigns and social media simultaneously, that representation becomes difficult to challenge because it seems to come from all directions at once.

A contested representation is one that actively challenges the dominant version. Contested representations can emerge from alternative or independent media, from social media campaigns, from documentary film-making, or from community-led journalism. They often come from members of the social group that has been misrepresented, who bring a different perspective and set of experiences to the production process.

Viewpoints, Values and Messages in Representation

Every representation communicates a viewpoint. This viewpoint may be explicit — a documentary that openly argues for a political position — or implicit, embedded in the choices of framing, language and selection that structure the product. Even apparently neutral factual products carry viewpoints: the decision to describe a protestor as an ‘activist’ versus a ‘campaigner’ versus a ‘troublemaker’ encodes a value judgement in a single word choice.

Representations become especially significant when the same viewpoint is reinforced across multiple media products and platforms, creating what scholars call a dominant ideology. Audiences are more likely to absorb and internalise an ideological position when it appears to come from everywhere independently rather than from a single source.

Key Fact

Dominant representations are repeated widely across media products and come to seem natural. Contested representations challenge dominant versions and often emerge from communities or producers with direct experience of the group being represented. Both carry viewpoints that reflect particular values and ideological positions.

The Rise of Self-Representation

For most of media history, representations of social groups were produced almost entirely by professionals working within large institutions. Ordinary people had no effective way to represent themselves to a mass audience. Digital technologies and social media platforms have changed this fundamentally. Today, individuals can produce, publish and distribute media content to potentially global audiences with minimal equipment and no institutional backing.

The term prosumer describes someone who is both producer and consumer of media. The rise of the prosumer has created new possibilities for self-representation: individuals and communities can now tell their own stories, challenge dominant representations of their social group, and reach audiences that would previously have been inaccessible.

Social media influencers represent a new kind of media producer. An influencer who belongs to a marginalised group and builds an audience around their own life and perspective is, in a real sense, producing a self-representation that would never have existed in legacy media. User-generated content (UGC) on platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram has enabled entirely new kinds of representation to enter the mainstream.

However, these possibilities have limits. Social media platforms are commercial organisations governed by algorithms that prioritise certain kinds of content and suppress others. Self-representations that are radical, uncomfortable or counter to mainstream tastes may find their reach restricted. The prosumer revolution does not dissolve institutional power — it creates new institutions with new gatekeeping mechanisms. The question of whose self-representation gets amplified, and whose gets buried, is as important as the question of who gets to speak at all.

The Social, Cultural and Political Significance of Representation

Representation matters far beyond the screen. When a social group is consistently represented in limiting, demeaning or absent ways, it affects how that group is treated in the real world. Research across sociology and psychology has shown that people’s attitudes towards groups they have little direct experience with are heavily shaped by media exposure. A group that is always shown as threatening in news media tends to be feared more in daily life; a group that is always invisible tends to be seen as marginal.

The social significance of representation is also about aspiration and identity. When young people see people who look like them, share their background or face similar challenges represented positively and centrally in mainstream media, it signals that their experiences are worth telling and their potential is recognised. Conversely, absence or exclusively negative representation sends the opposite message. This is why debates about diversity in casting, editorial leadership and production teams are not just about aesthetics — they have direct social consequences.

Key Fact

Representation has real social consequences: how groups are shown in media shapes audience attitudes towards those groups in daily life. Positive, complex representation enables aspiration and recognition; negative or absent representation can reinforce social inequalities and shape how groups are treated.

One of the most politically significant forms of representation is news. News organisations do not simply report what happens — they set the agenda by deciding which events are worthy of coverage and which are not. Scholars Johan Galtung and Marie Ruge identified a set of factors — news values — that make events more likely to be selected for news coverage: these include proximity (how close to the audience), magnitude (how big or dramatic), negativity (bad news travels faster than good), continuity (ongoing stories hold audience attention) and elite persons or nations (stories about powerful people or countries).

The political significance of news values lies in what they systematically exclude: small-scale positive stories, long-term structural problems without dramatic moments, and the experiences of groups that do not have elite status. This means the news as a whole represents a particular kind of world — one that privileges drama, crisis and power — which shapes how audiences understand politics, society and which groups matter.
exam_tip_html: In questions about viewpoints and self-representation, the highest-band answers connect individual examples to wider patterns. If you identify a self-representation on social media that challenges a dominant representation, explain why the dominant representation exists, what interests it serves, and why the self-representation is significant as a counter. For questions about the social significance of representation, avoid vague claims like “it makes audiences think X.” Be specific: which audiences, in relation to which social group, through which media product, producing which specific attitude or behaviour. The command word “evaluate” always requires you to consider both sides.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dominant representations are widely repeated and come to feel natural; contested representations challenge them, often produced by or with the social groups involved.
  • Digital technologies have enabled self-representation through UGC and the prosumer role, but platform algorithms and commercial pressures still limit which self-representations reach mass audiences.
  • Representation has real social, cultural and political consequences: it shapes attitudes, enables or restricts aspiration, and through agenda-setting determines which groups and issues seem important.

practice_questions.text: Which term describes a person who is simultaneously a producer and a consumer of media content?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: B) Prosumer. Distractors: A) Influencer; C) Gatekeeper; D) Broadcaster.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which digital technologies have enabled self-representation by individuals and communities.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Award for any valid example, e.g. ability to publish video content on social media platforms; creating a blog or podcast; posting directly to a global audience without institutional gatekeepers; developing an audience as a social media influencer.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why the social significance of representation extends beyond what is shown in media products.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct points: representation shapes audience attitudes towards groups they may have little direct experience of; negative representation can reinforce real-world discrimination; absence from representation can limit aspiration for members of under-represented groups; news agenda-setting shapes which issues people consider important.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'dominant representation' and why it can be difficult for contested representations to challenge it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear definition of dominant representation with specific features (repetition across many platforms, appears natural); clear explanation of why contested representations struggle (lack of institutional resources, algorithm suppression, small audiences) with at least one developed example.
Secure: Accurate definition; at least one reason for the difficulty in challenging dominant representations, with brief example.
Developing: Some understanding of dominant representation; challenge to it present but vague; limited example.
Emerging: Basic identification of some representations as powerful; limited understanding of why dominant versions persist.

practice_questions.text: Explain the concept of agenda-setting in news media and how it shapes representations of social groups, using an example from a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate definition of agenda-setting; clear explanation of how it shapes representation through selection of stories and prominence; Galtung and Ruge may be referenced accurately; specific example from a named product with detailed analysis of which groups are privileged or marginalised.
Secure: Accurate definition; representation implications present; at least one specific example with some development; theoretical reference optional but welcome.
Developing: Some understanding of agenda-setting; representation link present but undeveloped; one example present.
Emerging: Basic reference to news choosing what to cover; limited connection to representation; no specific example.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the social and political significance of representation in a media product you have studied. In your answer, consider how dominant and contested representations operate, and evaluate the impact of digital self-representation on the media landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained thesis on social/political significance; dominant and contested representations both addressed with specific analysis from a named product; digital self-representation evaluated with nuance (possibilities and limits); relevant theorists (e.g. Gerbner, Galtung and Ruge) applied accurately; coherent structure throughout; counter-position considered.
Secure: Clear argument addressing significance; both representation types present; digital self-representation discussed; examples anchor the analysis; some use of theory; well-structured.
Developing: Some understanding of social significance; at least one representation type addressed; digital self-representation mentioned; limited use of theory.
Emerging: Basic points about media representation having effects; mainly descriptive; limited specific examples; little or no theory.

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes a representation that is widely repeated and comes to seem natural across the media landscape?
Galtung and Ruge are associated with which concept in media studies?
The set of values, beliefs and assumptions reproduced across a wide range of media products, reflecting the perspective of the most powerful groups in society, is called the _____ ideology.
The process by which media organisations determine which issues are important by deciding what to cover is called _____.
Match each term to its correct definition.
right: A representation that challenges or opposes a dominant version, often produced by members of the represented group
Media content created by the public rather than professional producers, distributed through digital platforms
A person who is simultaneously a producer and a consumer of media content

flashcard_questions.a: A representation widely repeated across media that comes to feel natural and obvious
One that challenges a dominant version, often produced by or with the represented group

flashcard_questions.q: What is a viewpoint in media representation?
flashcard_questions.a: A particular perspective or set of values communicated through a media product
The values and assumptions of the most powerful groups, reproduced across many media products
A person who is both a producer and a consumer of media content
Content created by the public and distributed through digital platforms, not professional producers

flashcard_questions.q: What is agenda-setting in news media?
flashcard_questions.a: The power of news organisations to decide which issues receive coverage and prominence

flashcard_questions.q: Which scholars developed the concept of news values?
Name two news values identified by Galtung and Ruge.
flashcard_questions.a: Negativity and proximity (also: magnitude, continuity, elite persons)

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the social significance of representation extend beyond screen content?
flashcard_questions.a: It shapes real-world attitudes towards groups and affects aspiration and social inequality

flashcard_questions.q: What limits the reach of self-representation on social media platforms?
flashcard_questions.a: Commercial algorithms that prioritise certain content and suppress radical or counter-mainstream voices

glossary_terms.definition: Representations of a social group, place or issue that are widely repeated across the media landscape and come to feel natural or obvious.
A representation that challenges or opposes a dominant representation of a social group, place or issue, often produced by or with members of that group.
A particular perspective, set of values, or position on a social issue communicated through a media representation.
The set of values, beliefs and assumptions shared by the most powerful groups in a society and reproduced across a wide range of media products.
A person who is simultaneously a producer and a consumer of media content, enabled by digital technologies to create and distribute their own media to audiences.
Media content created by members of the public rather than professional media producers, distributed through digital platforms.
The process by which media organisations determine which issues are important by choosing what to cover and how prominently to cover it.
